# Title:ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
> Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns.
ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them.
Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

# The Path to Medical Superintelligence
## Medical Case Challenges and Benchmarks
To move beyond the limitations of multiple-choice questions, we’ve focused on sequential diagnosis, a cornerstone of real-world medical decision making. In this process, a clinician begins with an initial patient presentation and then iteratively selects questions and diagnostic tests to arrive at a final diagnosis. For example, a patient presenting with cough and fever may lead the clinician to order and review blood tests and a chest X-ray before they feel confident about diagnosing pneumonia.
To answer this, we created interactive case challenges drawn from the NEJM case series – what we call the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark (SD Bench). This benchmark transforms 304 recent NEJM cases into stepwise diagnostic encounters where models – or human physicians – can iteratively ask questions and order tests. As new information becomes available, the model or clinician updates their reasoning, gradually narrowing toward a final diagnosis. This diagnosis can then be compared to the gold-standard outcome published in the NEJM.
### Getting to a Correct Diagnosis
The best performing setup was MAI DxO paired with OpenAI’s o3, which correctly solved 85.5% of the NEJM benchmark cases. For comparison, we also evaluated 21 practicing physicians from the US and UK, each with 5-20 years of clinical experience. # MedRoundsQA: A Persona and Difficulty Aware Evaluation for Multi-Turn Medical Consultations
## Abstract
Medical benchmarks are dominated by single-turn, multiple-choice clinical cases that poorly reflect real consultations.  We introduce MedRoundsQA, a multi-turn diagnostic benchmark derived from 1,387 board-exam cases across 17 specialties. Each case is converted into a structured 24-slot clinical record, and then instantiated as controlled doctor-patient dual-agent dialogues under varying patient personas, with the underlying clinical content held fixed.
## Constructing a Controlled Clinical Dataset
MedRoundsQA contains 1,387 diagnostic cases from MedQA, NEJM diagnostic cases, and MedMCQA. The cases span 17 specialties and include 292 cases from MedQA, 646 from NEJM cases, and 449 from MedMCQA.
The authors compare GPT-4o, DeepSeek, and Claude on 100 manually annotated cases and select GPT-4o for large-scale extraction because it shows the strongest agreement across several lexical, semantic, embedding-based, and language-model judging measures. Three resident physicians then review the extracted records, correcting omissions, unsupported details, formatting errors, and hallucinated information.
## Difficulty, Human Comparison, and Error Patterns
On 60 difficult cases using the same simulated-patient interface, resident physicians achieve 48.33% accuracy, compared with 26.67% for the evaluated language models. Physicians use an average of 7.26 turns, while models use 12.32 turns. This comparison indicates that clinicians are more efficient at identifying high-value questions and consolidating evidence.
## Limitations and Overall Assessment
MedRoundsQA derives a substantial portion of its diagnostic cases from MedQA. This citation represents the exam-style, single-turn medical QA paradigm that MedRoundsQA extends into controlled multi-turn consultations.

+Follow on Google Add as preferred source Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published on Thursday in Science. The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an "orchestrator" that organises how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report. Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient's symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis. With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reach a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam. Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate. All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview. Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at "working up" the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet. The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions.

Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? We introduce ROUNDS, Reliability Of LLMs Under N-turn Diagnostic Scenarios, to examine whether models can diagnose without answer options and how they revise a diagnosis after receiving another person’s opinion (Figure 1). ROUNDS reuses the ordered evidence sequences constructed by MINT and presents them over multiple turns, with the diagnostic question appearing after the final evidence item (Fang et al., 2026). We then vary only the advice that follows, without adding clinical findings. One comparison presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing. Another presents written descriptions of five clinicians’ opinions and varies how many support the correct diagnosis. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, accuracy is lower without answer options for every model. The same wrong diagnosis lowers accuracy more under clinician framing than under lay framing. Initially correct diagnoses more often become incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopt the suggested disease. Accuracy also increases as more panel members support the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remains unchanged.

We use the ordered evidence sequences from MINT (Fang et al., 2026). Each turn presents the next part of the case, while earlier information and model replies remain in the conversation. This preserves the challenge of integrating later findings with an existing history, which can anchor models to earlier assumptions in multi-turn tasks (Laban et al., 2026).

keenable.snippet: Literature-derived cases are increasingly used to benchmark diagnostic rankers and language models (Danis et al., 2025; Bridges et al., 2025; Reese et al., 2026). Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong results on medical benchmarks, yet prevailing evaluations rely on a passive, full-context paradigm where complete information is provided upfront, failing to reflect clinical practice where information is scarce, cues are ambiguous, and clinicians must proactively elicit and verify evidence. Such static designs bypass the most critical stage, active evidence-seeking, and systematically overestimate model capability. We introduce ROUNDS-Bench, which decouples information-acquisition strategy from diagnostic reasoning and uses a standardized patient simulator to reconstruct multi-turn active evidence-seeking diagnostic processes including history-taking, physical exam, and test ordering. Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

Abstract: Clinical diagnosis at hospital admission must be made rapidly from limited, incomplete evidence. Existing diagnosis-prediction benchmarks are poorly suited to this setting: they restrict prediction to closed code sets, exclude free-text notes, and supervise with discharge diagnoses that incorporate the full inpatient course. We introduce EarlyDx, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended early diagnosis, built from 154,834 emergency department encounters in MIMIC-IV. Each encounter is restricted to records available at admission time $t_0$ and supervised by the diagnoses recorded during the ED encounter rather than at discharge. An LLM auditor further verifies every free-text label as supported, partially supported, or unsupported by that evidence; the primary evaluation scores only fully supported labels. Under a semantic LLM-as-judge protocol, no evaluated system --- frontier general, medical-specialized, or in-domain post-trained --- synthesizes admission-time evidence reliably. Zero-shot models score largely by extraction, recovering only 3-31% of diagnoses that must be inferred rather than read from the record; post-training raises inference-dependent recall to 56%, but a sizeable margin remains, and on time-critical conditions no system attains a clinician's balance of sensitivity and precision. ## What is a disease odyssey, and why study it?

A disease odyssey is the search for an explanation for perplexing symptoms: moving from unresolved findings to a diagnosis and, where possible, to treatment that alleviates symptoms or addresses their cause. Not every patient experiences a prolonged search, but disease-specific studies show that it can last months or years. In a U.S. claims study of 538 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, the median interval from the first recorded symptom claim to the first pulmonary-hypertension-related diagnosis was 8.3 months. In another U.S. study, 35.3% of 11,793 patients with endometriosis had an interval of three to five years between their first recorded symptom and diagnosis. These estimates describe recorded encounters in selected populations, rather than the full journey from symptom onset.[1, 2]

This period of search consumes clinical time and resources as clinicians order tests, consider competing explanations, and revise their judgments. seltz.snippet: Medical benchmarks are dominated by single-turn, multiple-choice clinical cases that poorly reflect real consultations. Practically, clinicians elicit evidence interactively, and patient communication varies widely. We introduce MEDROUNDSQA, a multi-turn diagnostic benchmark derived from 1,387 clinical cases across 17 specialties. Each case is converted into a structured 24-slot clinical record and then instantiated as controlled doctor–patient dual-agent dialogues under varying patient personas, with the underlying clinical content held fixed. Evaluations of fifteen LLM doctor agents show that (i) moving from a single-turn diagnosis on the standardized records to multi-turn consultations causes large degradations of roughly 13–39 points; (ii) more turns reliably improve question relevance, but diagnostic accuracy exhibits diminishing returns and typically plateaus after 6–12 turns; and (iii) patient persona differences can shift diagnosis accuracy by about 7–8 points from the lowest to highest education levels, highlighting equity risks that single-turn benchmarks miss.

ultimate.title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
ultimate.snippet:
We introduce ROUNDS, Reliability Of LLMs Under N-turn Diagnostic Scenarios, to examine whether models can diagnose without answer options and how they revise a diagnosis after receiving another person’s opinion (Figure 1). ROUNDS reuses the ordered evidence sequences constructed by MINT and presents them over multiple turns, with the diagnostic question appearing after the final evidence item (Fang et al., 2026). We then vary only the advice that follows, without adding clinical findings. One comparison presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing. Another presents written descriptions of five clinicians’ opinions and varies how many support the correct diagnosis. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, accuracy is lower without answer options for every model. The same wrong diagnosis lowers accuracy more under clinician framing than under lay framing. Initially correct diagnoses more often become incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopt the suggested disease. Accuracy also increases as more panel members support the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remains unchanged.

We use the ordered evidence sequences from MINT (Fang et al., 2026). Each turn presents the next part of the case, while earlier information and model replies remain in the conversation. This preserves the challenge of integrating later findings with an existing history, which can anchor models to earlier assumptions in multi-turn tasks (Laban et al., 2026).

ultimate.title: Observed, Curated, Reused: Observation Bias in Clinical AI Evaluation
ultimate.snippet: Literature-derived cases are increasingly used to benchmark diagnostic rankers and language models (Danis et al., 2025; Bridges et al., 2025; Reese et al., 2026). The rankers we study are not trained on patients in the usual machine-learning sense. They take a patient’s symptoms, written as HPO terms (Gargano et al., 2024), compare them with the symptom profile that HPO keeps for each disease, and return the diseases in order of how well they match. Everything such a ranker knows comes from these profiles, and each entry in a profile cites its source, often a published case report. In these evaluations, a single publication can supply both the patient features used to construct a test query and the disease–phenotype annotations used to rank diagnoses. Consider a case report describing a child with a rare disorder.

This benchmark transforms 304 recent NEJM cases into stepwise diagnostic encounters where models – or human physicians – can iteratively ask questions and order tests.
The MAI Dx Orchestrator turns any language model into a virtual panel of clinicians: it can ask follow-up questions, order tests, or deliver a diagnosis, then run a cost check and verify its own reasoning before deciding whether to proceed. While real-world health costs vary across geographies and systems, and include many downstream factors that we don’t account for, we apply a consistent methodology across all agents and physicians evaluated to help quantify high level trade-offs between diagnostic accuracy and resource use. For us, this is just the first step. We’re energized by the opportunities ahead. Important challenges remain before generative AI can be safely and responsibly deployed across healthcare. We need evidence drawn from real clinical environments, alongside appropriate governance and regulatory frameworks to ensure reliability, safety, and efficacy.
Without such constraints, an AI system might otherwise default to ordering every possible test – regardless of cost, patient discomfort, or delays in care.
